title: Learning to read from a theater saxophonist in Minneapolis
summary: A pit-band saxophonist gets him through a big study book; his bugle-horn transposition carries over to alto, and Thomas credits mathematics and Schillinger.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Minneapolis was a good town... Now, if I'd have had any sense, I'd have went to the University of Minneapolis [sic: U. of Minnesota], because I could have worked my way through! Because I knew how to go out and get a job and pay the tuition. But I just didn't want to ask my people for no more money, because they had put me through high school, and I figured I could make it on my own.

But the one thing that happened to me in Minneapolis, I went to a saxophone teacher, and he really got me straight. He got me the big Clozet(?) book and told me, he said, "If you go and read everything in this book, you won't hardly find nothin' you can't read." So I went through that book. I read...
Do you remember that guy's name?
No, I wished I could. He was playing in the band in the theatre.
In the Orpheum?
Thomas - 43

Yeah. And I remember that... Now, I don't know how I had that. But I had that little thing to study. It was way back in my younger days. And I remember he got me started, because he taught me how to read. And then I... That transposition... When I changed from C-melody to alto, I had to transpose. And I knew how to transpose!
That was going back the fluegelhorn.

Yeah. I mean, it wasn't no different. The transposition was just to alto instead of the fluegelhorn. And I learned how to transpose. This music was in me. I didn't know it until I got involved with it.
Well, it's your mathematics that was important to it.
Yeah.
The relativity of things.
Boy, you hit it on the head. Because man...
There are a lot of parallels there.
Yeah. That math just equalized everything. Because the whole note, half-note, quarter-note, eighth-note...
Sure. It ain't but one or two things. It's either got to be one, two...
Well, Schillinger said there's only three, and everything else is derivation from it.
Thomas - 44
That's right. So that's how simple you can bring it down to.
Yes. And boy, he did so much for me.
He sure did.
Boy, this guy was amazing... I talked to Eddie Barefield quite a bit about it, and Eddie was telling me, "He knew you wasn't no musician, but he just knew how to adapt..."
He's not a musician.
Right. It didn't matter.
